title: Stellar spectra, HR diagram and stellar evolution
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: A02-uk1#t1 term and clue written for the game; A02-uk1#t4 term and clue written for the game; A02-uk1#t2 term and clue written for the game; A02-uk1#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: A02-uk1#N.4b, A02-uk1#N.6, A02-uk1#N.7, A02-uk1#N.8.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Continuous spectrum
items.clue: Unbroken band of light emitted by the dense, hot surface of a star.

items.label: Energy levels
items.clue: Each element has its own set of these, fixing which photons its atoms absorb.

items.label: Diffraction grating
items.clue: Device giving bright maxima where d sin θ = nλ, with red further out than violet.

items.label: Zero order
items.clue: Straight-through maximum where all wavelengths overlap, showing the source's own colour.

questions.stem: A student looks at an unknown source through a diffraction grating. At the centre she sees a white line. On each side, she sees a full band from violet to red, crossed by a few thin dark lines. What is the source?

options.text: A low-pressure gas in a discharge tube
A white lamp shining through a cooler gas
A white lamp on its own
A salt heated in a flame, with no lamp behind it

questions.explanation: The lamp gives every wavelength (the band); the cooler gas absorbs its own wavelengths (the dark lines).

questions.stem: A star's continuous spectrum has dark lines at 410, 434, 486, 589.0, 589.6 and 656 nm. Laboratory emission lines: hydrogen 410, 434, 486, 656 nm; sodium 589.0, 589.6 nm; helium 447, 588, 668 nm. What can be deduced?

options.text: Hydrogen and sodium are in the outer layers; helium is not detected.
Hydrogen, sodium and helium are all present, as helium's 588 nm line is close to 589 nm.
Hydrogen and sodium are absent, so light at their wavelengths is missing.
Hydrogen and sodium in the star's core emit light at these six wavelengths.

questions.explanation: Every hydrogen and sodium line has a dark line at the same wavelength. Helium's 447 nm line has no match, and 588 and 668 nm are not where the star's lines are.

questions.stem: A star's spectrum has a dark line at 589 nm. What energy gap in the absorbing atoms does it match?

During a total solar eclipse, the Moon just covers the Sun's bright, dense surface, but the Sun's thin outer atmosphere still shows round the edge. A spectrum of that thin rim is taken. What does it show?

options.text: A continuous spectrum crossed by the Sun's usual dark lines
Nothing, because the atmosphere absorbs light and does not emit any
Bright lines at the same wavelengths as the Sun's usual dark lines
Bright lines at different wavelengths, unique to emission

questions.explanation: The atmosphere's atoms re-emit the photons they absorb. Seen against a dark sky, they give an emission line spectrum at the same wavelengths.
